title: Paul Speaks for the Weak
english: … would the One who knows all things have laid on us the yoke of the law, which so well directs what pleases him and trains us toward what is profitable, if he had known that we were caught in the nooses of Fate? Either let our opponents say that God did not know this; or, if they have chosen to think rightly and are deeply afraid to pour ignorance over his ineffable glory, they say that he gave laws, and indeed they will plainly confess that he fixed the penalties for wrongdoers. Then surely he knows that man lives with a free mind and is able to move by voluntary inclination toward whatever he wishes, with nothing to hinder him.

That is why the inspired Paul said that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives (Romans 7:1). He does not say such things, then, as though the human mind were subject to the nod of others. Rather, he reasons as a philosopher and examines closely the passions of human nature. He all but digs out with precision the sicknesses that reach inward to the mind, and he brings a charge against the body for its inborn love of pleasure, very fittingly taking on himself the part of one who is still sick with love of the flesh.

For though he himself had been crucified to the world, and the world to him (Galatians 6:14), and was truly worthy of admiration, he still thought it wise not to look to his own gift, but to make the weakness of those not yet like him the necessary subject of his discourse.

So when you hear him say, “For what I am doing, I do not understand” (Romans 7:15), think of certain exceedingly great sinners who suppose that they are living the truly best life, and that nothing could equal the luxury and the fleeting things of this world. They loathe the ways of decency, but they take pride in their own pleasures and wallow in them without restraint. It is of them, I think, that Paul says, “Those who set their minds on earthly things, whose god is the belly, and whose glory is in their shame” (Philippians 3:19). These people, carrying out what is base as though it were something highly praised, might fittingly say, “For what I am doing, I do not understand.”

Let them hear, then: “Wake up, you drunkards, from your wine” (Joel 1:5). For just as lovers of drink and the drunken, their clear thinking impaired by the passion, would not know what they were doing while they were drunk, so those whose minds have grown sick from love of the flesh and the most shameful pleasures would not know what they are doing at all. So Paul is explaining to us a disease of the human heart when he says, “For what I am doing, I do not understand.”

But suppose there is someone who offers a tenderer heart, as it were, to the reproofs of conscience, who is grieved that he does wrong, yet is still overpowered by the pleasures that lead to sin, and goes toward wrongdoing as if against his will. He might fittingly say, “For I do not practice what I want, but I do what I hate” (Romans 7:15). How many people, how many times, have admired self-control, and even begun the practice of it, and then been overcome by the goads of loathsome pleasure; and with their mind giving way to the worse, they have committed the …

Closing cut: ἐνηργήκασι τὴν breaks before its noun; ἁμαρτίαν opens u05-rem-mid. Rendered 'they have committed the …' so no word is added from the next section.
The numerals 205, 206 and the stray '13' are page/sheet markers in the copy-text and are not translated.
ὁ πάντα εἰδώς ('the One who knows all things') is God; capitalized 'One'.

γράφεται (middle) is the legal term 'to indict'; rendered 'brings a charge against'. τὸ πρόσωπον … περιτιθείς = 'taking on himself the part (role)', Cyril's reading that Paul speaks in the person of the weak, not of himself.
ἐξιτηλία ('fading, transience') rendered 'the fleeting things'; no extra noun such as 'pleasures' added.
In the Philippians quotation ὁ θεός refers to the belly, so 'god' stays lowercase.
παρακεκομμένοι (literally 'debased, counterfeited') rendered 'impaired' for the mind's lost precision (τὸ ἀκριβές).

βραβεύοντα and παιδαγωγοῦντα are accusative and agree with τὸν … ζυγόν, so the yoke of the law (not God, who is nominative ὁ πάντα εἰδώς) is what directs and trains; τὸ αὐτῷ δοκοῦν is 'what pleases him' (God). The tutoring image recalls the law as παιδαγωγός (Galatians 3:24) but is not a quotation, so it is not cited inline.

title: The Flesh Overpowers the Willing Mind
english: … sin, but afterward they are filled with dejection. It would be quite fitting for these people, who have grown weak almost against their will, to say in turn, “But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Romans 7:17).
“Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good” (Romans 7:16).

Again he turns the precision of his inquiry to the nature of the body, and examines the power of the sicknesses that are in it by nature. For the appetites that carry us off toward every kind of passion, and the faults of a pleasure-loving life, have their source in the flesh. The Savior’s disciple confirms us in this when he says, “Where do wars and where do quarrels among you come from? Do they not come from here, from your pleasures that wage war in your members?” (James 4:1).
“For willing lies close at hand for me, but accomplishing the good I do not find” (Romans 7:18).

“For willing,” he says, “lies close at hand for me, but accomplishing the good does not,” and so on. To show that the flesh stands accused, since it is in terrible labor with sin within itself, he wisely grants that the good lies close at hand for us, but not also the power to carry it through. For the flesh forces the mind, against its will, to turn aside where it does not wish to go. So as far as the mind’s own choice went, it would be free even of sin. But since it suffers an overpowering that is hard to escape, the blame would rightly belong not so much to the mind as to what overpowers it. That is why he says, “Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Romans 7:20).

But someone might say: suppose some wicked barbarians laid waste a city or a country, then took some of its inhabitants as captives of the spear and laid on them the yoke of slavery, and those who suffered this yielded by necessity to the bonds and laws of their masters. Would they deserve blame and indictment because they are not stronger than necessity, and do not strive to carry out what pleases themselves in defiance of the authority of those who have seized power over them? No one, I think, could fairly find fault with them. For they serve as slaves because they cannot be set free, and they yield, as I said, to misfortunes they did not want. They are distressed that they have been robbed of freedom, but, overcome by necessity by those who are stronger, they serve against their will. Now if this is not far from reason, let the human mind be acquitted of any charge over the sicknesses of the flesh.

“But it was in its power,” someone says, “not to choose to do it; for it holds the reins of its own will.” Then let it be stronger than that overpowering and free from the tyranny of sins. But if the nature of the flesh is hard to bear and hard to resist, stirring up untamed pleasure against the mind, and the law is too slow to help (for it does not have the power to put sins to death), no one could justly accuse the mind of failing to do the better thing and let go of the more shameful, even if it does perhaps hold the reins of the will within us.
“So I find this law: that when I want …” (Romans 7:21)

Source spelling ἠσθηνηκόσι read as ἠσθενηκόσι (perfect participle of ἀσθενέω, 'grown weak').

Subjects made explicit where the Greek leaves them to context: καταβιάζεται has 'the flesh' as subject and 'the mind' (τὸν νοῦν) as object; the following ἦν ἂν ἔξω καὶ ἁμαρτίας and αὐτοῦ refer to the mind. Rendering names 'the flesh' and 'the mind' for clarity, without adding new content.
δεσμοῖς τοῖς τῶν κρατούντων … νόμοις rendered 'the bonds and laws of their masters'; the Greek may also be read as 'the binding laws'. Sense unchanged.
ἀλλ' ἦν ἐπ' αὐτῷ, φησί is an objector's reply (φησί with an implied subject), not Paul; rendered 'someone says'. Cyril then answers it (οὐκοῦν ἔστω …).
πλεονεξία here is 'being overpowered, getting the upper hand' (cf. πλεονεκτούμενος earlier), not 'greed'.
σάρξ rendered 'flesh' and νοῦς 'mind' consistently; θελήματα 'will' (collective) in the reins image.

παράκειται in Romans 7:18 (and in Cyril's τὸ παρακεῖσθαι … τὸ ἀγαθόν) reads 'lies close at hand', matching Romans 7:21 in u05-rem-close and the same verse in u06-open and u06-rem-early, so Paul's repeated verb reads the same across the book.

title: The Law Advises but Cannot Redeem
english: “…to do what is good, evil lies close at hand for me” (Romans 7:21). Notice again how wisely and skillfully he approves of the law: not as able to blunt the sting of sin, nor as capable of putting to death the sin within us, but only as instilling into the mind the knowledge of what is beneficial. For if, he says, evil lies close at hand for me as something that dwells in the flesh, the law nonetheless exposes it as counterfeit; it grants its help and is understood as a counselor, but not also as a redeemer.

Yet those who are sick with sin surely need not only to know clearly that they ought to do what is better, but also to be able to accomplish whatever is good and seems right to the law. So too, of course, for those who wish to win distinction in battle, bare knowledge of tactics alone is not enough; only if strength is added to it would such men then, and scarcely then, be brilliant and admired. If, then, the law teaches skill in what is good, but in no way helps those who are overpowered by cutting the sinews of sin, it is good because it is also a teacher; but it could not fairly be counted equal to the grace that comes through Christ, who is able both to make us wise and to make us stronger than evil.

“For I delight in the law of God in my inner self” (Romans 7:22). As I have already said, the mind thirsts for freedom, longs to be rid of what stands condemned, and crowns the law with the highest honors as the guide to what is noblest; but the nature of the flesh forces it toward disordered pleasures, while the law of sin wages war and presses hard upon it (Romans 7:23). By the law of sin he means the inborn impulse, and whatever one might suppose the passion of love for the flesh to be, just as he called the law of the mind its inclination and will toward the good.

“Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death? I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:24–25). For now he laments and cries out against the flesh; and he calls the earthly, pleasure-loving body a “body of death,” because in it the law of sin is a sickness. He says that he seeks the one who is able to free us from such evils, and he does so in order to bring in the Redeemer for us at a fitting moment, that is, Christ, to whom he also gives all thanks. For through him we have been redeemed, not from the flesh but from the death of the flesh; not by dying, but by being set free from the death in our members, that is, from the savage pleasure in our members. For Christ has made us stronger than pleasure and sin.

“So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Romans 7:25). “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the spirit” (Romans 8:1). Section opens mid-lemma: the first words complete Romans 7:21, begun at the close of u05-rem-mid; rendered with a leading ellipsis.
κατακιβδηλεύει (lit. 'debases, adulterates'): rendered 'exposes it as counterfeit', the sense required by the contrast with the law's role as counsellor.
καταβιάζεται (middle, active sense, as in u06-open κατεβιάζετο… ἡ σάρξ): 'forces it', the object being the mind of the preceding clause.
ἐκτόπους ἡδονάς: 'disordered pleasures' (lit. 'out-of-place'); kept the same in u06-rem-early.
ὁμολογεῖ χάριν after εὐχαριστῶ: χάρις here is gratitude, so 'gives all thanks', not 'grace'.

τοῦ καὶ σοφοῦν ἰσχύοντος καὶ … ἀποφαίνοντος is genitive masculine and agrees with Χριστοῦ, not with the dative feminine χάριτι, so it is Christ 'who is able both to make us wise and to make us stronger than evil' (matching κρείττους γὰρ ἡμᾶς ἀπέφηνεν ὁ Χριστός below).
Page numbers 208, 209 and the footer '15' are edition apparatus and are omitted.
Section ends mid-sentence (οὓς ὑπομένειν ἔθος τὴν | ἀνθρώπου διάνοιαν); the sentence continues at the start of u06-open. English word order forces the split at 'which it is usual for the…'.
'According to the spirit' in Romans 8:1 is printed lowercase: in u06-open Cyril reads πνεῦμα here as the spiritual will of the human mind, its inclination toward the good.
